Brand: Dior (category: Fashion, Apparel & Footwear)
Topic from the client: repair and reuse

Please prepare an idea development worksheet for one campaign for this brand on this topic. The worksheet has these sections:

1. task_understanding: the problem or opportunity the campaign focuses on, and the assumptions about the brand, topic and audience.
2. candidates: exactly 4 candidate campaign directions whose core ideas differ from each other (not just different executions of one idea). For each: the core idea, how it connects to the brand, expected strengths and main concerns.
3. selection: which candidate is recommended and why, and for every other candidate why it was not recommended.
4. revisions_after_selection: changes made to the recommended idea after reviewing it, with the reason for each. Use an empty list if there are none.
5. final_proposal: the recommended idea written for a human reader (at most 150 words), plus exactly 3 open questions that would help the reader develop further ideas of their own.

Write in English. Return the worksheet as a single JSON object with this structure and nothing else:
{
  "task_understanding": {"focus": "...", "assumptions": ["..."]},
  "candidates": [
    {"id": "C1", "title": "...", "core_idea": "...", "brand_connection": "...", "expected_strengths": ["..."], "main_concerns": ["..."]},
    {"id": "C2", "...": "..."},
    {"id": "C3", "...": "..."},
    {"id": "C4", "...": "..."}
  ],
  "selection": {"selected_id": "C?", "reasons_for_selection": ["..."], "rejected": [{"id": "C?", "reason": "..."}]},
  "revisions_after_selection": [{"change": "...", "reason": "..."}],
  "final_proposal": {"title": "...", "idea": "...", "follow_up_questions": ["...", "...", "..."]}
}

task_understanding.focus: Make repair and reuse feel like the highest expression of Dior craft rather than a sustainability add-on or a sign that a piece is past its best. The opportunity is to move Dior from 'buy new, keep perfect' to 'a Dior piece is never finished', so the house's atelier skill is visible and desirable at the moment a piece is mended, altered or passed on.
assumptions: Dior is a luxury house whose authority comes from couture, the atelier and the 'petites mains', so the repair story should come from craft rather than from compliance or guilt.
Dior already offers some after-care and repair, but it is little known and seen as a back-of-house service. The campaign can reframe it without needing a new business model.

The audience is two groups. Existing clients with pieces in the wardrobe (Lady Dior, Saddle, Bar jacket) are the primary group. Aspirational younger luxury buyers who shop resale and vintage are the second.
Luxury sustainability messaging is crowded with vague claims, so a credible idea has to be tangible, experiential and specific, and must avoid unverifiable environmental statements.
The brand must not appear to promote damage or encourage owning more. The tone stays elevated, precise and emotional rather than activist.
Dior can mobilise its heritage assets: the archives, the Avenue Montaigne address, the toile (muslin prototype) process and the founder's lucky symbols.

candidates.title: Re-Toile
candidates.core_idea: In couture, every garment begins as a toile, a draft that is refined until it is right. Re-Toile treats every Dior piece the same way: never finished, always open to its next draft. Clients bring in any Dior piece, such as a faded Saddle, a loosened Bar jacket or a lining that has worn through. The atelier mends or re-drafts it, and the piece comes back with a small muslin-white 'second draft' signature stitch and a numbered label (Draft 2, Draft 3).
candidates.brand_connection: It uses Dior's own process language (toile, atelier, the fitting) and the founder's belief that clothes are constructed with intention. Repair becomes the continuation of couture rather than a service desk.
expected_strengths: A proprietary, ownable mechanic: the draft stitch and numbered label make repair visible, collectable and status-bearing.
Platformable across film, atelier events, social storytelling, retail service and archive exhibitions.
Reframes an 'old' item as a continuing piece without any anti-consumption messaging.
Builds long-term client relationships and repeat visits.
main_concerns: Atelier capacity and turnaround times could limit scale.
'Toile' is insider jargon and needs a simple public translation.
Needs a clear policy on what counts as repair versus redesign.

candidates.title: Petites Mains, Signed
candidates.core_idea: Put the anonymous artisans in the spotlight. Every repair is signed by the specific atelier hand who did it, with a short film, a handwritten note and a portrait of the craftsperson. A 'repair counter' on Avenue Montaigne is staged as a performance space where visitors watch a mend in progress.
candidates.brand_connection: It builds on Dior's most human asset: the skilled hands behind the glamour.
expected_strengths: Emotional, humanising and highly shareable documentary content.
Strengthens perceived value of craft and justifies the price of luxury.
Easy to produce and to localise.
main_concerns: 'Celebrating the artisan' is a well-worn luxury trope and is less surprising.
Focuses on the maker, not on what the owner gains by repairing.
May feel like heritage storytelling without a behaviour change.

candidates.title: Wardrobe Wills
candidates.core_idea: Invite owners to write a short 'will' for a beloved piece: who inherits it and what story goes with it. The atelier prepares the piece for its handover by restoring it, re-lining it and adding the heir's initials. Handovers are documented as intimate ceremonies, and the stories form a public archive of Dior pieces across generations.
candidates.brand_connection: It links Dior's heirloom-quality icons (the Lady Dior, the Bar jacket) to family and memory, positioning them as legacy objects.
expected_strengths: Deeply emotional and rich in human stories.
Naturally encourages reuse through inheritance and gifting.
main_concerns: Skews toward older, wealthier clients and may feel remote to younger audiences.
The 'will' framing can feel morbid and needs careful tone.
Limited ongoing repair behaviour between handovers.

candidates.title: The Mended Show
candidates.core_idea: A couture presentation built entirely from clients' worn, damaged or dormant Dior pieces, re-drafted by the ateliers into new looks and shown on a runway alongside the season's collection. The owners sit in the front row next to the guests.
candidates.brand_connection: It puts repair on the biggest stage Dior owns, the runway, and treats clients as co-creators of the house's legacy.
expected_strengths: Challenges the idea that the runway must always show new things.
main_concerns: One-off event that is hard to sustain as a platform.
Risk of being read as a stunt or as 'upcycling' without a service behind it.
Significant production cost and complexity, and mixed signals if shown beside new collection pieces.

reasons_for_selection: It is the only candidate that turns repair into an ongoing, ownable system (the draft stitch, the numbered label and the Draft language), so it can run for years rather than as a single moment.
It is rooted in a true product and process insight: couture is built on drafts, so 'never finished' is authentic to Dior rather than borrowed from sustainability language.
It reframes repair as status and progression ('my Draft 3') instead of wear and tear, which solves the central perception problem.
It contains the strengths of the other ideas: the atelier hands from C2, the passing-on from C3 and a runway or exhibition moment like C4, but all of them become expressions of one idea.
It is operationally credible because it builds on existing atelier skills and after-care.

rejected.reason: Strong emotional content but a familiar craft-celebration approach. It lacks a distinctive behavioural hook for owners and is better used as a content layer inside the chosen idea.
Emotionally rich but narrower in audience and with a potentially morbid tone. It drives handover rather than everyday repair, so it works better as a later chapter of the platform.
Spectacular but a one-off with high cost and a risk of being read as a stunt. It works best as a showcase moment for the chosen idea instead of the core.

revisions_after_selection.change: Replaced the jargon 'toile' in consumer-facing language with 'Draft' (for example 'Draft 2'), keeping 'Re-Toile' as the house and press name.
revisions_after_selection.reason: 'Toile' is understood by couture insiders but not by the second audience of younger resale-minded buyers. 'Draft' is instantly clear and keeps the creative metaphor.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added a clear scope: Re-Toile covers restoration and light re-drafting that preserves the original piece, and does not include destructive redesigns.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Protects the integrity of archival and collectible pieces, avoids overpromising to clients and keeps atelier workload manageable.

revisions_after_selection.change: Added an accessible entry tier: a short, quick 'first stitch' repair for small items such as straps, buttons and linings, with a fixed turnaround and a transparent price.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Atelier capacity is the main risk and a luxury-only service would exclude younger buyers. A simple tier widens reach and creates a first positive repair experience.

revisions_after_selection.change: Removed any environmental claims from the campaign and focused on craft, longevity and the owner's story.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps the work credible and avoids greenwashing risk, while still delivering the reuse outcome.

revisions_after_selection.change: Positioned the atelier hands, heirloom handovers and a runway or exhibition moment as later chapters of the platform, not as separate campaigns.
revisions_after_selection.reason: Keeps a single clear idea while keeping the best elements of the rejected candidates.

final_proposal.title: Re-Toile: Nothing Dior is ever finished
final_proposal.idea: Couture begins with a toile, a draft refined until it is right. Re-Toile gives that logic to every Dior piece you already own. Bring in a tired Saddle bag, a loosened Bar jacket or a worn lining and the atelier mends or re-drafts it. It comes back with a muslin-white stitch and a numbered label: Draft 2, Draft 3. Repair stops being a sign of age and becomes a sign of a piece worth continuing. A quick 'first stitch' tier makes the service easy to try, and the atelier hands, handover stories and a showcase moment follow as chapters of the same idea. The message is that Dior is never finished, so neither is your Dior.
follow_up_questions: What would the visible sign of a repair need to look like so that owners show it off rather than hide it?
Which first-time repair moments, such as a broken strap or a worn lining, could become the most emotional and shareable stories for younger audiences?
How could the 'Draft' idea extend beyond repair, for example to resale, gifting or archive pieces, without losing its meaning?
